title: Eating and drinking less, then trouble swallowing

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no contributor interview, no claim of corpus completeness.
limitations: This record is not a nutrition or hydration decision guide.
Sources are public patient/family-facing; oral testimony is needed for bedside conflict and cultural variation.

moment.plain_scene: A dying person becomes less interested in meals or drinks, takes only small sips or soft foods, and later may have trouble swallowing food, fluids, or oral medicines.
ordinary_language_queries: not eating at end of life

content_layers.observation_text: Public sources describe eating and drinking less as common when someone is dying, with eventual difficulty swallowing food, fluids, and oral medicines in some contexts. Family-facing sources emphasize dry mouth care and small amounts only when appropriate and wanted.
content_layers.source_synthesis: NHS Inform, NCI, and Hospice UK converge on reduced intake and swallowing changes, while also distinguishing comfort measures such as mouth care from forcing food or drink. NCI notes that supplemental nutrition does not benefit patients in the last days of life and can introduce risks in that context; this requires clinical review before public rendering.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: This moment is emotionally loaded because feeding is care in many families. The future corpus should document the family conflict, love, guilt, and cultural meaning around food separately from clinical explanations.

what_this_is_not: not a rule that food or fluids should be withheld
not an instruction to stop medicines
not a substitute for clinical assessment of nausea, pain, constipation, choking, dehydration concern, or reversible causes
uncertainties: Food and drink practices vary widely across families and traditions.
The sources do not capture the emotional and moral pressure families may feel.
Clinical decisions about nutrition, hydration, and medication routes are context-specific.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should validate that food refusal can be deeply upsetting, describe the observed pattern, and route questions about comfort, swallowing, medicines, or fluids to the care team.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner surface should collect how workers explain reduced intake, mouth care, swallowing risk, and the distinction between comfort and prolongation without shaming families.
language_notes: Ordinary-language search phrases are retained as search aliases, not as diagnostic labels.
Professional terms are index handles; they do not collapse all contexts into one cause or one meaning.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the v2 witnessed-moment schema. It should be reviewed before any public surface uses it.

safety.clinical_boundary: This record is observational/source-indexing only. It is not medical advice, not a prognosis, and not a substitute for a local hospice, clinician, emergency, or care team.
safety.safety_notes: Before public use, route through clinical safety review and ensure lay surface directs urgent or worried readers to qualified local support.
